passages.original: a discendo au:em penitus impediebar, ad quod mihi tota intentione animi opus erat : tamen mihi videbatur, si se ille mentibus meis veritatis falgor aperiret, aut me non sensurum fuUse illum dolorem, aut certe pro nihilo toleraturum. Sed quia etsi nihil majus aliquando pertuli, tamen sæpe cogitans quanto graviores possint accidere, cogor interdum Cornelio Celso assentiri, qui ait summum bonum esse sapientiam, summum autem malum dolorem corporis. Nec ejus ratio mibi videtur absurda. Nam quoniam duabus, inquit, partibus compositi sumus, ex animo scilicet et corpore, quarum prior pars est animus melior, deterius corpus est;
passages.english: but I was completely prevented from learning, for which I needed the whole attention of my mind. Yet it seemed to me that if that brightness of truth were to open itself to my mind, either I would not have felt that pain, or at any rate I would have endured it as nothing. But although I have never suffered anything greater, still, often thinking how much heavier [pains] could befall [me], I am sometimes compelled to agree with Cornelius Celsus, who says that the highest good is wisdom and the highest evil is bodily pain. Nor does his reasoning seem absurd to me. For since, he says, we are composed of two parts, namely of soul and body, of which the former part, the soul, is the better, and the body is the worse;
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently: 'au:em' (autem), 'falgor' (fulgor), 'fuUse' (fuisse), 'mibi' (mihi). 'mentibus meis' (literally 'my minds') is rendered 'my mind'. The sentence beginning 'But although...' is grammatically loose in the Latin ('Sed quia etsi... tamen... cogor'); translated by sense.
